title: The Subjunctive --- the Mood of the Not-Yet-Real

lessons.title: Hablas español, Quiero que hables español — fact or wanted event?
lessons.headword: Hablas español · Quiero que hables español
lessons.romanization: Hablas español · Quiero que hables español
lessons.gloss: an asserted event beside a wanted, not-yet-real event

segments.text: Hablas español can assert “You speak Spanish.” Now compare Quiero que hables español — “I want you to speak Spanish.” Hables does not report what is true. It presents the speaking as wanted and not yet asserted. That meaning contrast is the first small doorway into the subjunctive.

utterances: meaning: I want to speak Spanish. Spanish: Quiero hablar español. doers: one: I want; I speak.
meaning: I want you to speak Spanish. Spanish: Quiero que hables español. doers: two: I want; you speak.

segments.text: With one doer, keep the known infinitive hablar. With a different doer for the wanted event, use que and the new form hables. This is a bounded pattern for querer, not a rule for every clause in Spanish.

segments.prompt: Which form asserts that one friend speaks: hablas or hables?

feedback.correct: Right: hablas can assert the event.
feedback.incorrect: Use indicative hablas for the asserted event; hables is the wanted form here.

segments.prompt: Say 'I want to speak Spanish' in Spanish.

feedback.correct: Right: one doer keeps the infinitive hablar.
feedback.incorrect: Use known quiero plus the infinitive: Quiero hablar español.

segments.prompt: Say 'I want you to speak Spanish' to one friend.

feedback.correct: Right: two doers give quiero que hables.
feedback.incorrect: Join the wanted event with que and use hables: Quiero que hables español.

segments.text: Which form asserts the event? (Hablas.) Which presents it as wanted? (Hables, after quiero que.) What happens when the wanter and the speaker are the same? (Use the infinitive: Quiero hablar.) Next, build the three singular -ar forms one piece at a time.

lessons.title: hable, hables, hable — the singular -ar row
lessons.gloss: the singular present subjunctive of hablar

segments.text: You already used hables for one friend. Today add only the other two singular slots:

utterances: person: yo. present subjunctive: hable.
person: tú. present subjunctive: hables.
person: él / ella / usted. present subjunctive: hable.

segments.text: Plural forms wait. Say the small row: hable, hables, hable.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the yo stem, then a vowel swap

segments.text: Start from present hablo. Remove -o to reveal habl-. Regular -ar verbs then use e in these subjunctive endings: -e, -es, -e. The family vowel has swapped from the familiar a to e. This recipe will matter later because a verb's special present yo stem can travel with it.

Spanish subjuntivo descends from Latin subiūnctīvus, “subjoined,” from sub- “under” plus iungere “join.” English join, junction, and conjunction belong to the same word family; yoke is a more distant cousin. The name helps you picture the wanted clause joined under quiero que. It is history, not a complete usage rule.
Build each answer only from the learned singular row.

segments.prompt: Give the learned singular present-subjunctive forms of hablar: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Use the e-family row: hable, hables, hable.

segments.prompt: Which present form gives the stem for regular hable: hablo or habla?

feedback.correct: Right: remove -o from hablo to get habl-.
feedback.incorrect: Start from the present yo form hablo, then remove -o.

segments.prompt: What joining idea sits inside the Latin source of subjuntivo?

feedback.incorrect: Think of a clause joined under another: subjoined.

segments.text: Give the three forms. (Hable, hables, hable.) Which present form supplies the stem? (Hablo.) What did the family vowel do? (a becomes e.) What does the name remember? (A clause subjoined, or joined under another.)

lessons.title: coma, comas, coma — let -er cross to a
lessons.gloss: the singular present subjunctive of comer

segments.text: Start from como, remove -o, and keep com-. A regular -er verb crosses to the a family:

utterances: person: yo. present subjunctive: coma.
person: tú. present subjunctive: comas.
person: él / ella / usted. present subjunctive: coma.

segments.text: Say only the singular row: coma, comas, coma.

Comes can assert “you eat.” Quiero que comas presents your eating as what I want. The e becomes a contrast helps you hear the two meanings. It does not mean that every a form is subjunctive; use the learned frame as a whole.
Keep comer inside the learned singular frame.

segments.prompt: Give the learned singular subjunctive forms of comer: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Use the a-family row: coma, comas, coma.

segments.prompt: Which form belongs after quiero que for one friend: comes or comas?

feedback.correct: Right: quiero que comas presents the eating as wanted.
feedback.incorrect: Use subjunctive comas after the learned trigger quiero que.

segments.prompt: Say 'I want you to eat' to one friend.

feedback.incorrect: Use the two-doer frame quiero que plus comas.

segments.text: Give the three forms. (Coma, comas, coma.) Which form asserts “you eat”? (Comes.) Which belongs after quiero que? (Comas.) Next, test whether regular -ir behaves differently.

lessons.title: viva, vivas, viva — -ir joins -er
lessons.gloss: the singular present subjunctive of vivir

segments.text: Start from vivo, remove -o, then add the same a endings you just used with comer:

utterances: person: yo. present subjunctive: viva.
person: tú. present subjunctive: vivas.
person: él / ella / usted. present subjunctive: viva.

segments.text: Regular -er and -ir match in this singular row: coma/comas/coma and viva/vivas/viva. Plural differences wait.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: meaning in a known frame

segments.text: Vives en Madrid asserts where one friend lives. Quiero que vivas en Madrid makes that living a wanted event. Nothing new is being smuggled into the sentence: en and Madrid have appeared in the earlier location frame.
Keep vivir inside the learned singular frame.

segments.prompt: Give the learned singular subjunctive forms of vivir: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Use the a-family row: viva, vivas, viva.

segments.prompt: Which two regular verb families share -a, -as, -a here?

feedback.correct: Right: regular -er and -ir match in the learned singular row.
feedback.incorrect: Coma and viva reveal the pair: -er and -ir.

segments.prompt: Say 'I want you to live in Madrid' to one friend.

feedback.correct: Right: Quiero que vivas en Madrid.
feedback.incorrect: Use quiero que plus the tú subjunctive vivas, then en Madrid.

segments.text: Give the three forms. (Viva, vivas, viva.) Which regular family matches -ir here? (-er.) Which form fits one friend after quiero que? (Vivas.)

lessons.title: quiera, quieras, quiera — keep the change you know
lessons.gloss: the singular present subjunctive of querer

segments.text: Present quiero already carries the stressed e becomes ie change. Remove -o to get quier-, then add the -er/-ir subjunctive endings:

utterances: person: yo. present subjunctive: quiera.
person: tú. present subjunctive: quieras.
person: él / ella / usted. present subjunctive: quiera.

segments.text: Say only this bounded singular row: quiera, quieras, quiera.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one known verb, one inherited stem

segments.text: You are not learning a new list of stem-changing verbs. You are carrying one known change into one known row. Quiero que quieras hablar español means “I want you to want to speak Spanish.” The sentence is deliberately narrow: no new person noun, object, or plural form.
Carry only the known quier- stem into this row.

segments.prompt: Give the learned singular subjunctive forms of querer: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Keep quier- and add -a, -as, -a.

segments.prompt: Which known present yo form gives the stem quier-?

feedback.incorrect: Start from the learned yo form quiero.

segments.prompt: Complete 'Quiero que ___ hablar español' for one friend.

feedback.correct: Right: Quiero que quieras hablar español.
feedback.incorrect: Use the tú subjunctive of querer: quieras.

segments.text: Give the three forms. (Quiera, quieras, quiera.) Which old change stays visible? (e becomes ie.) Where did the stem come from? (Known quiero, minus -o.)

lessons.title: pueda, puedas, pueda — one more known stem change
lessons.gloss: the singular present subjunctive of poder

segments.text: Present puedo already carries o becomes ue. Remove -o to get pued-, then add the same a row:

utterances: person: yo. present subjunctive: pueda.
person: tú. present subjunctive: puedas.
person: él / ella / usted. present subjunctive: pueda.

segments.text: Say pueda, puedas, pueda. No other poder forms enter today.

Quiero que puedas hablar español means “I want you to be able to speak Spanish.” Every word was already known except the single form puedas. This is the gentle pattern: learn one row, then spend it in the next sentence.
Carry only the known pued- stem into this row.

segments.prompt: Give the learned singular subjunctive forms of poder: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Keep pued- and add -a, -as, -a.

segments.prompt: Which known present yo form gives the stem pued-?

feedback.incorrect: Start from the learned yo form puedo.

segments.prompt: Say 'I want you to be able to speak Spanish' to one friend.

feedback.correct: Right: Quiero que puedas hablar español.
feedback.incorrect: Use quiero que plus puedas, then known hablar español.

segments.text: Give the three forms. (Pueda, puedas, pueda.) Which old change stays visible? (o becomes ue.) Which form addresses one friend after quiero que? (Puedas.)

lessons.title: haga, hagas, haga — hago lends its stem
lessons.gloss: the singular present subjunctive of hacer

segments.text: The known present yo form is hago. Remove -o and keep hag-:

utterances: person: yo. present subjunctive: haga.
person: tú. present subjunctive: hagas.
person: él / ella / usted. present subjunctive: haga.

segments.text: Say haga, hagas, haga. Only hacer enters this lesson; other special stems wait for later chapters.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: spend the new form

segments.text: Haces café can assert “you make coffee.” Quiero que hagas café says “I want you to make coffee.” The g is not a fresh exception: it was already in hago, the present form that supplied the stem.
Carry only the known hag- stem into this row.

segments.prompt: Give the learned singular subjunctive forms of hacer: yo, tú, then él/ella/usted.

feedback.incorrect: Keep hag- from hago and add -a, -as, -a.

segments.prompt: Which known present yo form gives the stem hag-?

feedback.incorrect: The stem comes from the learned yo form hago.

segments.prompt: Say 'I want you to make coffee' to one friend.

feedback.incorrect: Use quiero que plus hagas, then known café.

segments.text: Give the three forms. (Haga, hagas, haga.) Where does hag- come from? (Known hago, minus -o.) Say the wanted event. (Quiero que hagas café.)

lessons.title: ojalá + subjunctive — a wish borrowed through Arabic
lessons.gloss: a wish trigger borrowed through Hispanic Arabic

segments.text: Ojalá hables español means “I hope you speak Spanish” or “May you speak Spanish.” Ojalá expresses the wish by itself. It needs neither a main verb nor que before the subjunctive. Keep the first frame tiny:
Ojalá + subjunctive.
That is a usable modern pattern. It does not make the Arabic source phrase new Spanish vocabulary.

The Real Academia Española records ojalá from Hispanic Arabic wa šá lláh, “and God has willed.” Long contact in al-Andalus carried the expression into Spanish, where its sound and grammatical life changed. You met another Arabic-derived function word in hasta. The historical phrase explains a route; only modern ojalá is available for your Spanish sentences.
Use only modern ojalá as the Spanish trigger.

segments.prompt: Say 'I hope you speak Spanish' to one friend using ojalá.

feedback.incorrect: Use ojalá directly before the tú subjunctive hables.

segments.prompt: Does the learned ojalá frame require que before hables? Answer yes or no.

feedback.correct: Right: ojalá directly licenses the subjunctive in this frame.
feedback.incorrect: No: say Ojalá hables, without que.

segments.prompt: Through which historical language variety did Spanish receive ojalá?

feedback.correct: Right: the recorded route is through Hispanic Arabic.
feedback.incorrect: The historical route named here is Hispanic Arabic.

segments.text: What follows ojalá in the learned frame? (The subjunctive.) Does it need que? (No.) Which historical language variety carried the word into Spanish? (Hispanic Arabic.) Is the older Arabic phrase usable as new Spanish vocabulary here? (No.)

lessons.title: Practice — assert the event or want it
lessons.gloss: a singular checkpoint for wanted events and the present subjunctive

segments.text: This checkpoint adds no vocabulary, plural person, object pronoun, or new clause frame. First decide whether the event is asserted or wanted. Then retrieve only the singular rows you learned.

utterances: verb: hablar. yo / él / ella / usted: hable. tú: hables.
verb: comer. yo / él / ella / usted: coma. tú: comas.
verb: vivir. yo / él / ella / usted: viva. tú: vivas.
verb: querer. yo / él / ella / usted: quiera. tú: quieras.
verb: poder. yo / él / ella / usted: pueda. tú: puedas.
verb: hacer. yo / él / ella / usted: haga. tú: hagas.

segments.text: The repeated outer form is not a missing row: first- and third-person singular match. Every plural form waits.
Same doer: Quiero hablar español.
Different doer: Quiero que hables español.
Wish by itself: Ojalá hables español.
Do not extend these two frames to every emotion, doubt, command, or conjunction yet. More triggers belong in later micro-lessons.
Decide the meaning first; then retrieve only the learned form.

segments.prompt: Choose the wanted-event form: hablas or hables.

feedback.correct: Right: hables is the wanted-event form in this chapter.
feedback.incorrect: Hablas can assert; hables follows the learned wish frame.

segments.prompt: Give the pair 'I want to speak Spanish; I want you to speak Spanish.'
acceptedResponses: quiero hablar español; quiero que hables español.
quiero hablar español quiero que hables español
quiero hablar español / quiero que hables español

feedback.correct: Right: one doer uses hablar; two use que hables.
feedback.incorrect: Use Quiero hablar español, then Quiero que hables español.

segments.prompt: Give the tú subjunctive forms of hablar, comer, and vivir, in that order.

feedback.incorrect: Retrieve the three tú forms: hable-s, coma-s, viva-s.

segments.prompt: Which present-person form supplies the stem in this chapter's recipe?

feedback.correct: Right: start from the present yo form.
feedback.incorrect: The recipe begins with the present yo form.

segments.prompt: Give the learned singular subjunctive row of querer.

feedback.incorrect: Keep quier- and add -a, -as, -a.

segments.prompt: Say 'I want you to be able to speak Spanish' to one friend.

feedback.correct: Right: Quiero que puedas hablar español.
feedback.incorrect: Use quiero que plus puedas, then hablar español.

segments.prompt: Say 'I want you to make coffee' to one friend.

feedback.incorrect: Use quiero que plus hagas, then café.

segments.prompt: Say 'I hope you live in Madrid' to one friend using ojalá.

feedback.incorrect: Use ojalá directly before vivas en Madrid.

segments.prompt: What does the Latin source subiūnctīvus help you picture?
acceptedResponses: a clause subjoined or joined under another

feedback.incorrect: It carries the idea of being subjoined, or joined under another.

segments.prompt: Name the historical language variety through which ojalá entered Spanish.

feedback.incorrect: The route recorded here is Hispanic Arabic.

segments.text: What is the first meaning choice? (Asserted event or wanted event.) Give the three regular tú forms. (Hables, comas, vivas.) Give the three bounded special tú forms. (Quieras, puedas, hagas.) Name the two safe triggers. (Quiero que for a different doer; ojalá for a wish.) What still waits? (Plural persons, additional irregular verbs, and additional subjunctive triggers.)
